notes.text:
A third instance of the same family, from operating the board on 2026-09-03 — worth folding in here
because the cause is shared: **an operator edit cannot land before the tick acts on it.**

`hkb create` without `--triage` files a card *ready*, and the loop claims it inside 60 s. So the natural
sequence "file the card, then link its dependency" loses the race, and the card is already running against a
graph that is about to change. Three times tonight:

- **#303** — claimed before I could point it at #325.
- **#305** — claimed, and one minute into renaming every `src/*.js` to `.ts`, before I could sequence it
  behind #304. It had already written to disk.
- **#330** — claimed before the link to #304 landed.

Each recovery is the same five commands: `hkb block --kind transient`, `hkb unblock`, `claude stop`,
`git worktree remove -f -f`, `claude rm`.

The operator workaround is real but easy to forget: file with `--triage`, link, then `promote`. Three
commands where one should do, and the failure mode when you forget is a worker doing withdrawn work.

**What would fix it**, roughly by how much each helps:

1. `create --blocked-by` already exists; the gap is filing a card that is *ready but not yet claimable*. A
   `--hold` flag — or making `create` land held until the next explicit `promote` — closes it.
2. More generally, the tick claims on a board read that may be seconds stale. A claim could re-check the
   card's graph immediately before spawning; it already holds the board, so this is cheap.
3. The mirror-image case, same root: a card being worked cannot be corrected at all, because the brief is
   assembled at claim time — an operator comment posted during a run reaches nobody. That cost me two
   corrections tonight that landed after the worker had taken its context. Related to #222; probably wants
   its own card once it costs something real.

Fourth instance, and the first one that cost an hour rather than minutes — which changes what this card is
about.

**#304, 2026-09-03.** Attempt 1 ran ~1 h and was reclaimed when its Claude session daemon died
(`control.sock` ENOENT), leaving three good commits and 13 uncommitted files in its worktree and no PR.
I pushed the branch and posted a note telling the next attempt where the work was and not to start over.
The note landed at 10:56:58. Attempt 2 had claimed at **10:56:11** — 47 seconds earlier. So it never saw
it, and was about to redo the whole docs half from scratch.

Recovering meant `block --kind transient` → `unblock` → `claude stop` → `git worktree remove -f -f` →
`claude rm`, throwing away a minute of live work to save an hour of duplicated work.

**The sharper statement of this card's family: `hkb` has no channel to a card between claim and finish.**
The brief is assembled once, at claim. After that every mechanism the operator has — `comment`, `edit`,
`link`, `adopt` — writes to a card the worker has stopped reading. The only way to change what a running
worker knows is to kill it and re-dispatch, which costs its progress and its context.

That is worth more than the promote-warning this card was originally filed for. The claim race
(three earlier instances, above) is one symptom; a worker that cannot be told "your predecessor's work is on
this branch", or "stop, the plan changed", or "the answer to your blocked question is X", is the general
case. Note `hkb block --kind needs_input` already implies the reverse channel exists in one direction only:
a worker can ask, and then must die to hear the answer.

**Worth considering** (this card, or a new one it points at):
- The Stop hook already runs in the worker's session. A `notes since claim` read at that point would at
  least let a worker see an operator message before it finishes, which covers the "your work is preserved"
  and "the plan changed" cases without any new transport.
- `hkb heartbeat` is the one verb a worker already calls mid-run, and it already returns a result object.
  It could carry pending operator notes back, making the existing beat the channel.
- Neither needs a daemon, a socket, or a new dependency — which matters, because the reason attempt 1 died
  in the first place was a daemon socket going away.
